item.title: The Cradle
item.lesson: At the scandalous first Impressionist exhibition of 1874, one painter in the group was a woman: Berthe Morisot, granddaughter (by family tradition) of Fragonard, who had turned down the safety of the Salon to throw in with the rebels. The Cradle shows her sister Edma watching her sleeping daughter through a veil of gauze — and it is worth knowing that Edma had also been a gifted painter, one who gave up art on marrying, as respectable women were expected to do. Morisot paints her sister's gaze as something layered: tenderness, absorption, and perhaps something more complicated behind the resting hand. The translucent curtain is a bravura performance — paint describing fabric you can see through — and it doubles the picture's meaning: mother and child separated by the thinnest of veils, intimacy and distance at once. Morisot exhibited in seven of the eight Impressionist shows, missing one only for the birth of her own daughter.
item.lookFor: Follow the diagonal from Edma's eyes through her propped hand to the baby's bent arm — the infant unconsciously mirrors her mother's pose, a rhyme Morisot surely watched happen in life.
